headnote: A stoppage may only be deducted from laytime when the express contractual condition for the exception is satisfied. The master's subjective view that conditions were unworkable is not enough; the contract's threshold (e.g. precipitation > 0.5 mm/hr) must be met on the facts.

A vessel becomes an 'arrived ship' for NOR purposes when she has reached a position within the port where she is at the immediate and effective disposition of the charterer. The classical 'Reid test'.

Distinguishes a port charter from a berth charter for the purposes of NOR; under a port charter the vessel need only be within the legal/commercial limits of the port to tender NOR, provided she is at the charterer's effective disposition.

citation: Sociedad Financiera de Bienes Raices SA v Agrimpex (The Aello) [1961] AC 135
headnote: Earlier statement of the 'arrived ship' doctrine, since modified by The Johanna Oldendorff; useful for tracing the evolution of the test.

citation: Compania de Naviera Nedelka v Tradax (The Tres Flores) [1973] 2 Lloyd's Rep 247
headnote: Notice of readiness is invalid if at the time of tender the vessel is not in fact 'ready in all respects' to load or discharge, including holds being clean and fumigated.
Exception clauses are construed strictly against the charterer who seeks to invoke them. Ambiguity in the exception language is resolved in favour of the owner.

citation: Union of India v Compania Naviera Aeolus (The Spalmatori) [1964] 2 Lloyd's Rep 415
headnote: Tender of NOR before free pratique can be valid where free pratique is a mere formality on the facts; the rule is fact-sensitive and the formality must be likely to be granted on application.

citation: Channel Island Ferries Ltd v Sealink United Kingdom Ltd (The Forum Craftsman) [1985] 1 Lloyd's Rep 291
headnote: Once a vessel is on demurrage, exceptions to laytime no longer apply unless the charter party expressly extends them to demurrage; the 'once on demurrage always on demurrage' principle.

citation: President of India v Lips Maritime Corp [1988] AC 395
headnote: Demurrage is liquidated damages for detention of the vessel beyond the agreed laytime; it is not freight nor a separate cause of action for breach.

citation: Compagnie Generale Maritime v Diakan Spirit SA (The Bonde) [1991] 1 Lloyd's Rep 136
headnote: Despatch is calculated only against working time saved unless the charter party provides 'all time saved'; the wording is decisive.

When invoking a weather exception, the burden of proving the contractual condition (and the time it applied) rests on the party asserting the exception, supported by contemporaneous evidence (port logs, weather observations).
Time-bar clauses in charter parties are construed strictly; a claim presented out of time without compliance with the procedural requirements of the clause is barred regardless of merit.

citation: Nereide SpA di Navigazione v Bulk Oil International (The Laura Prima) [1982] 1 Lloyd's Rep 1
headnote: A charter party warranty that the loading berth is 'reachable on arrival' makes the charterer strictly liable for any delay in reaching the berth caused by berth congestion, independent of fault.
A 'WIBON' (whether in berth or not) clause does not by itself shift weather risk during the wait for berth; weather exception applies only when the vessel is actually working cargo.

citation: Case C-308/06 Intertanko and others [2008] ECR I-4057
headnote: CJEU on the relationship between MARPOL and Directive 2005/35/EC; the validity of EU rules going beyond MARPOL on ship-source pollution penalties cannot be challenged by reference to MARPOL itself.
